title: You cannot fold paper more than seven or eight times.
description:
You cannot fold paper more than seven or eight times. True for an ordinary sheet. It was never a law of mathematics, only a limit nobody had bothered to break.

A California high-school student solving a fold-count challenge for extra credit. She proved it first on a folded strip of gold, then set out to do it with paper.

She folded a single sheet twelve times. The sheet was a strip of tissue paper about 1,219 metres long, three quarters of a mile, because length is what a fold count actually costs.

How much more paper the twelfth fold consumes than the first, by Gallivan's own equation. Not a guess; exponential growth, counted.

She did not break the rule. She worked out why it existed.

Sources:
- https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/494571-most-times-to-fold-a-piece-of-paper: the official record entry, read in full. Establishes that Britney Gallivan, of Pomona, California, folded a single piece of paper in half twelve times on 27 January 2002, the first person to reach nine, ten, eleven and twelve folds; that the tissue paper used was 4,000 feet (1,219 metres) long; and that she derived her own equations for the minimum length needed for a given number of folds, published in her book 'How to Fold Paper in Half Twelve Times'.
- https://www.sciencenews.org/article/folding-paper-half-twelve-times: Ivars Peterson, Science News, 22 January 2004, read in full. Explains the folk belief that paper cannot be folded more than seven or eight times; that Gallivan was a high-school student solving the problem for extra credit and proved it first on a folded strip of gold before doing it with paper; and computes from her published equation that the twelfth fold consumes 2,798,250 times as much paper as the first.
